- When sentiment shows strong positive momentum (e.g., recent sentiment > 0.67 and rising), model tends to over-forecast; reduce forecast peak by 5–10% if sentiment is trending up.
- If sentiment turns negative or shows sharp decline (e.g., sentiment change < -0.5 or sudden drop), model often overshoots early and then falls; adjust forecast downward by 3–8% in the first 5–7 days after negative sentiment spike.
- Model consistently overestimates prices in the first 3–5 days after a sentiment spike, especially when news volume is high; apply a 5–10% downward correction for early forecast days post-spike.
- When sentiment is flat or mildly negative (0.33–0.67) and news volume is steady, model tends to underestimate; add 2–5% to forecast if sentiment is stable or mildly negative.
- Model exhibits mean reversion bias: if forecast is > 10% above recent 7-day average, reduce by 5–10% in next 3–5 days; if below, add 2–5% if sentiment is weak.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates in the first 10 days after a sentiment shift; apply a 3–7% downward adjustment for days 1–10 post-sentiment change.
- If sentiment change is > 0.5 and news volume is high, model tends to overreact; cap forecast at 10% below recent 14-day high if sentiment is rising sharply.
